title: Tata Sons Profit Climbs 22% but Air India Losses Double to ₹22,238 Crore
excerpt: The holding company's standalone net profit rose to ₹31,961 crore in FY26, even as its flagship airline posted a net loss of $2.32 billion and extended its turnaround timeline to a decade.
body:
• Tata Sons' standalone net profit rose 21.8% to ₹31,961 crore in FY26, while the broader group's profit surged 52% to ₹1.71 lakh crore.
  • Air India's net loss more than doubled to ₹22,238 crore ($2.32 billion), driven by airspace closures, high fuel costs and operational disruptions.
  • Chairman Chandrasekaran extended the airline's turnaround timeline to up to a decade, departing from the original five-year Vihaan.AI plan.
  • The group's unlisted ventures collectively lost over ₹10,905 crore in FY25, with internal estimates projecting losses widening to ₹29,000 crore in FY26.

Tata Sons, the holding company of India's largest conglomerate, reported a 21.8% rise in standalone net profit for the financial year ending March 2026, even as its most high-profile acquisition—Air India—sank deeper into losses, doubling its deficit to ₹22,238 crore ($2.32 billion).

The contrasting results, disclosed in Tata Sons' FY26 annual report released on July 28, underscore both the financial resilience of the Tata Group's established businesses and the mounting costs of its ambitious bets on aviation, semiconductors and digital platforms.

Record Profit at the Holding Company Level

Tata Sons' standalone net profit rose to ₹31,961 crore in FY26, up from ₹26,232 crore the previous year, while revenue climbed 9.1% to ₹42,367 crore. The board recommended a dividend of ₹1,10,717 per share.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=UJTr-nMMLQM

The broader Tata Group also recorded strong growth. Consolidated revenue crossed ₹16 lakh crore—more than doubling since FY20—while group-level profit after tax surged 52% to ₹1.71 lakh crore, lifted by strong performances across TCS, Tata Motors, Tata Steel, Titan and Indian Hotels.

"We are building capabilities for the India of 2047 by making sustained investments in sectors expected to drive the country's next phase of industrial and technological growth."

— N. Chandrasekaran, Chairman, Tata Sons

Air India: Losses Double, Turnaround Timeline Stretches

Air India, which Tata Group reacquired from the government in January 2022, posted a net loss of ₹22,238 crore in FY26, more than double the ₹10,859 crore loss recorded in FY25. The figures make the airline the group's single largest loss-maker by a wide margin.

The widening losses were driven by multiple headwinds: the closure of Pakistani airspace for Indian carriers, rerouted flights to Europe and the US due to Persian Gulf airspace restrictions, elevated fuel costs tied to the West Asia conflict, and the operational fallout from a deadly crash in 2025.

In a significant shift, Chairman Chandrasekaran acknowledged in the annual report that Air India's turnaround could take up to a decade—a departure from the Vihaan.AI five-year plan unveiled by then-CEO Campbell Wilson in September 2022. Wilson is set to step down on September 30, and Tata Sons has yet to announce a successor.

Singapore Airlines, which holds a 25.1% stake in Air India following the Vistara merger in 2024, reported its share of losses at S$945.2 million (US$742.4 million) for FY26, dragging on the Singaporean carrier's own earnings.

The Broader Investment Dilemma

Air India is not the only drain on Tata Sons' resources. The group's unlisted ventures collectively posted losses of over ₹10,905 crore in FY25, up sharply from ₹1,557 crore in FY20. Internal estimates suggest losses could widen to nearly ₹29,000 crore in FY26, with Air India and Tata Digital—which houses the Tata Neu super app—accounting for the bulk.

This has prompted governance concerns. Proxy advisory firm InGovern wrote to the boards of seven listed Tata companies, arguing that the current structure creates a "closed-loop system of capital consumption" where cash from listed companies funds long-gestation projects at the holding company level without adequate minority shareholder oversight.

Meanwhile, Tata Sons' dividend income from TCS—its largest cash generator—declined 12.1% to ₹28,292 crore in FY26, narrowing the financial cushion available for loss-making ventures.

Strategic Bets: AI, Chips and Defence

Despite the red ink, Tata Sons is doubling down on its forward-looking bets. The annual report highlighted investments across artificial intelligence, semiconductor manufacturing through Tata Electronics, electric mobility, defence and digital platforms as key pillars of future growth.

Tata Electronics, which acquired Wistron's Karnataka-based iPhone assembly unit and commenced production at a second facility in Tamil Nadu, posted a comparatively modest loss of ₹70 crore in FY25, positioning it as a near-term turnaround candidate among the group's newer ventures.

The group also pointed to milestones including Tata Capital's IPO, Tata Motors' demerger, record domestic deliveries at Tata Steel, Tata Power's renewable energy expansion, Titan's international growth and Indian Hotels' record financial performance as evidence of its diversified strength.

What's Next

The immediate focus will be on Air India's leadership transition and whether Tata Sons adjusts its capital allocation strategy under board pressure. With the airline's turnaround now framed as a decade-long project and Singapore Airlines reportedly in discussions with Tata Group about injecting fresh funds, the aviation bet remains the conglomerate's most consequential—and most expensive—strategic gamble.
nri_angle: Tata Group's financial performance directly affects millions of diaspora investors holding shares in listed companies like TCS, Tata Motors and Tata Steel, while Air India's service quality and route network shape the travel experience for NRIs flying to India.
